extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, grant program officers, and scholars who serve on or study grant peer-review panels
extracted.subtask_description: Norms and evaluative standards for how academic peer-review panels should judge fellowship/grant proposals and how panelists should behave during deliberations. Emphasizes procedural legitimacy, disciplinary pluralism, and pragmatic decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid strategic voting (high-balling vs low-balling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic voting is when panelists rank proposals to influence outcomes rather than on intrinsic merit. High-balling (assigning an unduly high rank) is sometimes considered permissible; low-balling (assigning an unduly low rank) is viewed as illegitimate because it unfairly penalizes otherwise strong proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'threes' (mid/low scores) can effectively end a proposal; low-balling is the only form of strategic voting panelists describe as illegitimate. Be cautious of deliberate low scores that kill proposals. Recognize that strategic moves are especially likely late in deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual (relational) ranking of proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate proposals relationally within the particular pool under consideration rather than as abstract, context-free objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists acknowledge scholarly quality is 'relationally defined within the universe of the group of proposals' and that the reference point shifts during deliberation. Practical decision-making often requires comparing differently flawed proposals and satisficing (selecting the best available).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketing self-interest and personal ties (recusal/abstention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal ties and self-interest are illegitimate influences; panelists are expected to abstain or recuse themselves when close colleagues, advisees, or people for whom they have written letters are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal rules typically require abstention for direct conflicts; many panelists also voluntarily recuse themselves for indirect/informal ties. Abstention preserves legitimacy, though those who recuse may feel slighted if their candidates are denied funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of informal ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists should disclose indirect or informal ties when they exist (e.g., 'this student’s mentor is a close collaborator of mine'), even if not formally required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such disclosures are common and customary. They help manage influence of networks, though they are not always offered systematically because ties are frequent in specialized fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate personal taste to professional/neutral criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists should distinguish between personal preferences and objective criteria of competence and privilege the latter when they conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'two sets of criteria'—professional judgment as neutrally as possible, and personal taste used only when it doesn't interfere. If other panelists' arguments seem sound, one 'should always give up the personal one.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive contextualization / methodological pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate proposals according to the epistemological and methodological standards of the applicant’s discipline rather than imposing a single cross-disciplinary standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists should be willing and able to 'understand the projects in their own terms.' Recognize that different methods serve different purposes; disciplinary sovereignty and pluralism bolster legitimacy even if they mean different standards are applied across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to expertise (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect and defer to colleagues' specialized expertise when appropriate, but do not acquiesce blindly when expertise is narrow, contested, or being used to push discipline-specific agendas outside their remit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference helps panels function, but may be withheld when a specialist focuses on obscure details or when multiple people claim overlapping expertise. Convincing at least two other panelists is typically required to sway the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set aside disciplinary prejudices and give distant disciplines benefit of the doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists should actively check and disclose biases favoring or disfavoring certain disciplines, and be willing to give far-removed disciplines extra benefit of the doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices include 'fessing up' to scoring biases and intentionally being 'a little bit harder' on one's own discipline to avoid reflexive favoritism. Panel composition diversity helps reduce the impact of individual prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pushing one’s own field or 'self-reproduction'
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists must avoid promoting their own discipline, school, or network for parochial reasons (e.g., sponsoring anything from a favored subfield regardless of merit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pushing one’s own field undermines credibility and can provoke distrust; earning credibility through respectful behavior increases a panelist’s ability to advocate successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain collegiality and respectful interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Uphold norms of courtesy, avoid offensive or aggressive conduct, and manage interpersonal tensions with 'emotion work' so the panel can reach consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaches of collegiality (e.g., 'in your face' responses, public humiliation) can derail panels and require program officers or chairs to repair relationships. Nonverbal cues (frowning, sighing) can be powerful; keep criticisms articulated and contestable rather than allusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage conflicts carefully to preserve panel functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: When disagreements arise—over eligibility, standards, or disciplinary overreach—use institutional mechanisms and chair leadership to resolve disputes without letting them contaminate the whole panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers and chairs may need to intervene; reintegrate upset panelists after defeat. Avoid letting early conflict set a pattern that skews subsequent deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent criteria where possible (qualitative vs quantitative fairness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive for consistency in applying standards across different methodological approaches, while still honoring discipline-specific norms; inconsistent application undermines legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tensions between qualitative and quantitative work are common; panelists should 'judge the proposals on their own turf' but also be mindful of comparability. Inconsistency in how criteria are deployed is a frequent source of dissatisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic about final-stage trade-offs and timing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that timing matters: end-of-panel negotiations (horse-trading, quid pro quo) and compromises are a pragmatic response to allocating the last awards among comparably flawed proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists may strategically negotiate to win priority for certain proposals; accept that 'satisficing' and bargaining are part of real-world decision-making, though these moves should be governed by norms of fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidentiality and exclude academic gossip
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep deliberations confidential, avoid sharing internal discussions with excluded parties, and do not use gossip as part of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers of letters who recused themselves may expect some explanation but panels typically do not disclose deliberation details. Upholding confidentiality preserves legitimacy and relationships.
